value.overview: The Double-striped Thick-knee is a large, ground-dwelling bird of open tropical landscapes. It is named for the prominent double-striped pattern on its head and the thick-looking joints of its long legs. Its mottled brown plumage provides excellent camouflage among dry grass, leaf litter, and bare soil. Usually active at dusk, at night, and around dawn, it is often found in pairs and is more frequently heard than seen.
value.classification: The Double-striped Thick-knee belongs to the family Burhinidae, the thick-knees or stone-curlews, within the order Charadriiformes. Its current scientific name is Hesperoburhinus bistriatus; older references commonly use Burhinus bistriatus.
value.identification: This is a tall, long-legged bird, approximately 45–50 cm long, with a bulky body, large yellow eyes, and a strong black-and-yellow bill. The upperparts are finely mottled grayish brown, while the underparts are paler. Key field marks include a broad white eyebrow, a dark stripe above it, and another dark facial stripe through the eye area. In flight, white wing markings contrast with darker flight feathers. Its upright posture and thick legs are distinctive.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America into northern South America, with additional populations in parts of the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is a resident but localized bird, recorded mainly in the Pacific lowlands, especially the dry northwest and other open areas of Guanacaste and Puntarenas. It uses dry forest edges, savannas, lightly grazed pasture, cultivated fields, ranchland, and other open ground with short vegetation. It generally avoids dense, closed forest and steep, heavily wooded terrain.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica, birds are present throughout the year in suitable lowland habitats, although local movements may occur when vegetation, water, or grazing conditions change.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place on the ground. The nest is usually a shallow scrape or minimally prepared depression in bare soil, gravel, or short vegetation, where the cryptic eggs and incubating adult blend with the surroundings. Pairs defend breeding territories and rely on camouflage rather than substantial nest construction. Both adults are involved in incubation and care of the young. Exact timing can vary geographically, and breeding records in Costa Rica are associated with open lowland habitats, particularly in the Pacific region.
value.dietFeeding: The Double-striped Thick-knee feeds mainly on insects and other terrestrial invertebrates, including beetles, grasshoppers, and similar prey. It may also take small vertebrates and other appropriately sized animals when available. It commonly forages by walking slowly across open ground, pausing to scan, then making short runs or pecks to capture prey. Its large eyes and crepuscular or nocturnal activity help it feed in low light.
value.behavior: This species is usually encountered singly, in pairs, or in small family groups. It spends much of the day resting quietly and relies heavily on camouflage, often crouching or standing motionless when approached. Activity increases around dawn, dusk, and at night. Its loud, far-carrying calls are characteristic of thick-knees and can reveal its presence before the bird is located. When disturbed, it may run rather than immediately fly.
